passages.happening:
Jesus finishes his teaching and leaves Galilee for the region of Judea beyond the Jordan River. Large crowds follow him, and he heals them there.

Some Pharisees come to test him. “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” (verse 3). Jesus answers from the beginning of the Bible. The Creator made them male and female, and a man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. “Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (verse 6).

“Why then,” they ask, “did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away?” Jesus replies that Moses permitted divorce because of their hardness of heart, “but it was not this way from the beginning” (verse 8). Then he says that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman, commits adultery.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this same debate (Mark 10:1-12), and the note on Mark 10 explains the background. The land beyond the Jordan was ruled by Herod Antipas, who had killed John the Baptist for speaking against his marriage. A question about divorce asked in Herod's land was a dangerous one.

Only Matthew has the words ‘for any reason’ in the Pharisees' question. Those words take us into an argument among Jewish teachers over Deuteronomy 24:1, which lets a man divorce his wife if he finds ‘some indecency’ in her. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, keeps the later memory of the debate (Gittin 9:10). The school of Shammai said a man could divorce only for something shameful, such as unfaithfulness. The school of Hillel said he could divorce even if she spoiled his dinner. A later teacher, Rabbi Akiva, said even if he found another woman he liked better. Josephus, writing in the first century, sums up the law as letting a man divorce his wife ‘for any cause whatsoever’ (Antiquities 4.253). So the question in Matthew asks Jesus to take a side. Some scholars think ‘for any reason’ was the very name of the easy divorce of Hillel's school, and that this is what Jesus answers. Others think Jesus' answer reaches further than that.

In Jewish law at that time, only the husband could end a marriage, by writing and handing his wife a certificate. A wife sent away could be left with nothing. That is the world Jesus spoke into.

Matthew also tells the debate in a different order from Mark. In Mark, Jesus asks what Moses commanded. In Matthew, Jesus goes straight to creation, and it is the Pharisees who bring up Moses. They say Moses ‘ordered’ a certificate. Jesus says Moses ‘permitted’ it. A rule that limits a wrong is not the same as a command to do it.
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two verses from the first pages of the Bible. Genesis 1:27: “male and female He created them.” And Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”

The rule the Pharisees quote is Deuteronomy 24:1-4. Read closely, it does not command divorce. It assumes divorce happens and puts limits on it. Through the prophet Malachi God says, “do not break faith” with the wife of your youth (Malachi 2:16).

‘Hardness of heart’ was a prophet's word for a people who would not listen. Ezekiel promised a day when God would take away “your heart of stone” and give “a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.hard:
Only Matthew has the words ‘except for sexual immorality’ (here and in 5:32). Mark, Luke and Paul give Jesus' teaching without them. Christians read the exception and the whole teaching in different ways, and each answer is held by careful readers. The Catholic Church teaches that a true sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved while both spouses live, though it allows separation and can declare that a true marriage never existed. Some Catholic scholars read the Greek word here as a marriage the law forbade, such as to a close relative. The Orthodox churches hold marriage to be for life but, as an act of mercy, allow a second marriage with a service of repentance. Most Protestant churches read the exception, with Paul's words about a spouse who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15), as showing that unfaithfulness and desertion can free the innocent partner to remarry. Many also count abuse as breaking the marriage covenant. Some read the exception as unfaithfulness during betrothal, as when Joseph planned to divorce Mary (1:19). These notes do not decide between them.

What all of them share is Jesus' main point. God meant marriage to last for life, and divorce is always a tearing of what he joined. In his world, Jesus' words also protected wives, who could be sent away with almost no say. He makes the husband answerable for what he does.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.
passages.asks: The Pharisees asked how far the rules would let a man go. Jesus asked what God intended. Ask where you look for the edge of the rules instead of the heart of the command. And if divorce has touched your life, by your choice or not, remember that Jesus spoke these words to defend the one with no power. He is not against you.

passages.t: Those who do not marry, for the kingdom
passages.happening:
The disciples are shaken. “If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry” (verse 10).

“Not everyone can accept this word,” Jesus answers, “but only those to whom it has been given” (verse 11). There are eunuchs who were born that way. There are others who were made that way by men. “And still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it” (verse 12).

These verses are found only in Matthew.
passages.hearers:
The disciples' reaction shows how strict Jesus' words sounded. If a man cannot send his wife away, they think, perhaps marriage is not worth the risk.

A eunuch was a man who could not father children. Some were born that way. Others had been castrated, often as slaves or as servants in a royal court. The Ethiopian official in Acts, “a court official in charge of the entire treasury” of the queen, was a eunuch (Acts 8:27). Jesus' first two kinds are real people the disciples would have known of.

The third kind is a picture. Literally Jesus says they ‘made themselves eunuchs’. He means people who give up marriage and children for the sake of God's kingdom, to be free for his work. In Jewish life this was very unusual. Marriage and children were expected of every man. Yet Jesus himself did not marry. Neither did John the Baptist. Paul, at least in the years of his travels, was single too, and he called it a gift: “each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that” (1 Corinthians 7:7).

The early church did not take the words about the body literally. Justin Martyr, writing in the 150s, tells of a young Christian in Alexandria who asked the Roman governor for permission to be castrated, and was refused (First Apology 29). Justin tells it to show how seriously Christians took purity, not to commend the act. In 325 the Council of Nicaea ruled that a man who had castrated himself could not serve as a clergyman.
passages.ot:
The Law had kept eunuchs out of Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). But Isaiah looked ahead to a day when that would change. “Let the eunuch not say, ‘I am but a dry tree’” (Isaiah 56:3). To the eunuchs who keep his covenant God promises “a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5).

A prophet could be called to stay single. God told Jeremiah, “You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place” (Jeremiah 16:2).
passages.hard:
What does ‘this word’ in verse 11 point back to? Readers differ. Many think it points to the disciples' remark that it is better not to marry, so that Jesus answers: yes, for some, as a gift. Others think it points back to his teaching on divorce, so that the saying is about those who, after a marriage has broken, stay unmarried. Both readings are held.

Christians have drawn different things from this saying. The Catholic Church teaches that priests of the Latin Church are normally chosen from men who live celibate lives ‘for the sake of the kingdom of heaven’, and it honours vowed religious life. The Orthodox churches ordain married men as priests and choose their bishops from among the celibate. Protestant churches have stressed verse 11, ‘not everyone can accept this word’. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 cited it against requiring all clergy to stay unmarried. What all agree on is that singleness for the kingdom is a calling to be honoured, not a lesser life, and that it is a gift some are given, not a rule for everyone.

A word to readers who are single. Some have chosen it for God's sake. Many did not choose it, or have not chosen it yet, or are single after loss. Some cannot marry for reasons they did not choose. This passage does not ask you to explain yourself. Jesus, who was single, speaks of singleness here with honour. A church that treats single people as unfinished, or as a problem to be solved, has not listened to him.
passages.asks: Jesus speaks of marriage and of singleness in the same breath, and both are callings before God. Ask whether you honour both in the way you speak about them. If you are single, ask what freedom for God's work your life holds now. If you are married, ask how you can make room in your life for those who are not.

passages.happening: Little children are brought to Jesus for him to place his hands on them and pray for them. The disciples rebuke the people who brought them. But Jesus says, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (verse 14). He places his hands on them, and then he goes on his way.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too, and the note on Mark 10 explains it. Children in that world had no rank and could give nothing back, and important men did not stop their work for them.

Matthew adds that the parents wanted Jesus to pray for the children, not only to touch them. Laying hands on a child and praying for them was the way an elder or a teacher blessed them.

Matthew leaves out two things Mark has: that Jesus was ‘indignant’, and his saying that whoever does not receive the kingdom like a child will never enter it. Matthew has already given that saying in another form, in the last chapter: “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (18:3). So this scene shows in action what Jesus taught there. The disciples who heard that lesson are already turning children away.
passages.ot: Laying hands on someone to bless them goes back to the patriarchs. When old Jacob blessed Joseph's two boys, “Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim” (Genesis 48:14). Jesus does what Israel's fathers did. He blesses the children.
passages.asks: The disciples thought they were protecting Jesus' time. Jesus said the children were the point. Ask who you might be keeping away from Jesus because they seem unimportant or in the way, in your church, your home, or your plans.

passages.t: The young man who went away sad
passages.happening:
A man comes to Jesus and asks, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?” (verse 16). “Why do you ask Me about what is good?” Jesus replies. “There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments” (verse 17).

“Which ones?” the man asks. Jesus names do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.

“All these I have kept,” says the young man. “What do I still lack?” Jesus tells him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me” (verse 21). When the young man hears this, he goes away sad, because he has great wealth.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story (Mark 10:17-22), and the note on Mark 10 explains it. Matthew tells it with differences worth noticing.

In Mark the man calls Jesus ‘Good Teacher’, and Jesus asks, ‘Why do you call Me good?’ In Matthew the man asks what ‘good thing’ he must do, and Jesus turns him from a good deed to the one who is good, God himself. Some later copies of Matthew changed his wording to match Mark. The oldest copies, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus among them, have the wording the BSB gives.

Only Matthew calls him ‘young’ (verse 20). Luke calls him a ruler (Luke 18:18). All three say he was rich.

Only Matthew adds ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ to the list of commandments. Matthew will later call it the second great command, on which, with love for God, all the Law hangs (22:39-40). The man says he has kept it. Jesus' answer shows what loving his neighbor would cost: give what he owns to the poor.

‘Perfect’ is the word Jesus used in the Sermon on the Mount: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (5:48). It means whole, complete, undivided. It is not a higher grade of holiness for a few. It is a heart not split between God and something else. For this man, the something else was his wealth.
passages.ot: The commandments Jesus names come from the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12-16), with the great command of Leviticus 19:18, “love your neighbor as yourself.” Moses promised blessing to those who obeyed (Deuteronomy 28:1-2), and many people took wealth as a sign of God's favor. That is part of why this scene, and the next, shocked the disciples.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus ask every Christian to sell everything? The church has read this in two ways. Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian teacher in Egypt, wrote a whole sermon on this passage, titled Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? He argued that Jesus asks us to be free from the love of money, not always to give it all away. Others have taken the words literally. A young Egyptian named Antony heard Matthew's version of this story read in church, gave away his family's land, and later went to live in the desert, as Athanasius tells in his Life of Antony. Many Christians since have followed one path or the other. Some have read verse 21 as a special call to a few who seek a fuller life of devotion, while most keep the commandments. Others have answered that Jesus gives no one a lower road: he named this man's idol, and he may name a different one for each of us.

Two wrong turns must be avoided. This story gives no ground for contempt toward people who are wealthy. Mark says Jesus “looked at him, loved him” (Mark 10:21), and the New Testament tells the rich to be “generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:18), not to be ashamed of existing. Nor does it teach that faith brings riches. The man walked away from Jesus because of what he had, not for lack of it.
passages.asks: The young man asked, ‘What do I still lack?’ and went away sad when he heard the answer. Ask what Jesus might name if you asked him the same question. It may not be money. It will be whatever holds the place that only he should hold.

passages.t: A camel and the eye of a needle
passages.happening:
Jesus tells his disciples that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. “Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (verse 24).

The disciples are greatly astonished. “Who then can be saved?” Jesus looks at them and says, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The note on Mark 10 explains the camel and the needle. The camel was the largest animal in the land, and the eye of a needle the smallest opening anyone knew. Jesus is describing something impossible. The Babylonian Talmud, written down several centuries later, uses an elephant going through the eye of a needle in the same way. You may hear that the ‘Eye of the Needle’ was a small gate in Jerusalem's wall. There is no ancient evidence for such a gate. Some later readers also suggested that ‘camel’ should be read as a similar Greek word for a rope. The oldest copies of Matthew read ‘camel’. Both ideas soften what Jesus said, and verse 26 shows he meant it to be impossible.

Notice that Matthew says ‘the kingdom of God’ in verse 24. Almost everywhere else he says ‘the kingdom of heaven’, a respectful Jewish way of speaking of God without saying his name too often. They mean the same thing.

The disciples' shock is real. If the rich, who could give to the poor and keep every feast, could not get in, who could?
passages.ot: Jesus' answer echoes the Lord's word to Abraham when Sarah laughed at the promise of a son in her old age: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). What is impossible for people is God's to do.
passages.hard: Is it wrong to be rich? Jesus does not say that wealth is evil. He says it makes entering the kingdom hard, so hard that only God can do it. Wealth tempts a person to trust what they own instead of God. But the answer in verse 26 is for everyone, rich or poor: no one gets in by their own strength. The poor are not saved by being poor either. Salvation is God's work for anyone.
passages.asks: Ask what you trust to make you safe: savings, skill, reputation, being good. Jesus says none of it can carry you through the needle. Then hear the hope in verse 26. If it is impossible, it is also God's to do, and he does it.

passages.t: We have left everything: the first and the last
passages.happening:
“Look,” Peter says, “we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?” (verse 27).

Jesus answers that “in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (verse 28). Everyone who has left houses or family or fields for the sake of his name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Peter's question is honest, and a little anxious. They have done what the rich man would not. What will it come to?

Here, on the road, the promise of twelve thrones is found only in Matthew. Luke gives a similar saying at the Last Supper (Luke 22:30). Israel was made of twelve tribes, but most of them had been scattered since the Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom long before. The prophets had promised that God would gather his scattered people and make them one nation again (Ezekiel 37:21-22). The Psalms of Solomon, a Jewish book written in the century before Jesus, pray for a son of David to come and rule. Jesus' twelve disciples stand for that gathered Israel. ‘Judging’ here means ruling and leading, as the judges of old did.

‘The renewal of all things’ is one Greek word, palingenesia, literally ‘becoming again’. It appears in the New Testament only here and in Titus 3:5. It points to the world made new at the end of the age, not to escape from it.

Mark's version of the promise adds “along with persecutions” (Mark 10:30). Matthew leaves those words out, but his Gospel has already warned that following Jesus brings hatred and loss (10:16-39).

Then the last line. ‘Many who are first will be last.’ It is a warning to Peter, who has just asked what he will get. And it is the door into the next story: the parable of the workers in the vineyard, which ends with the same words turned around (20:16).
passages.ot:
In Daniel's vision, “thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat” (Daniel 7:9), and one like a son of man was given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13-14). Jesus takes that title, the Son of Man, and says the throne is his.

‘Inherit’ is the language of Israel receiving the land as God's gift. Moses told the people to obey, “so that you may live and may enter and take possession of the land” (Deuteronomy 4:1). Now what is inherited is eternal life.
passages.hard:
The promise of a ‘hundredfold’ (verse 29) has been used to promise money to those who give to a preacher. The words do not allow that reading. The houses and brothers and sisters are the new family of believers, who share their homes and lives. In Mark's version Jesus adds ‘along with persecutions’. No one selling a get-rich promise mentions that.

Nor is the promise of thrones a reason for pride. The next words put the first last. And the one who will sit on the glorious throne is walking to Jerusalem to die. As Paul said, “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).
passages.asks: Peter kept a tally of what he had given up. Jesus did not scold him; he promised more than Peter could count. Then he warned him about counting. Ask whether you keep accounts with God, and what it would look like to follow him without them.
